title: Hallucination Assessment via Log-probs as Time Series
one_line_claim: Log-probability sequences treated as time series can detect hallucinations in LLM outputs using a lightweight GRU, without requiring access to hidden states or external validators.
method_summary: HALT extracts the top-20 token log-probabilities from LLM generations as sequences and feeds them to a bidirectional GRU with entropy-based summary statistics (mean log-prob, rank proxy, decision entropy, temporal changes) to predict hallucination scores. The approach operates on token-level logit distributions rather than hidden states or text content, enabling black-box deployment on proprietary APIs.

key_findings.finding: HALT achieves 30x parameter reduction compared to fine-tuned ModernBERT baselines while outperforming them, and delivers 60x speedup over the Lettuce baseline.
key_findings.quote: HALT is a 5M-parameter GRU model that outperforms a fine-tuned ModernBERT encoder 30x larger. We release two HALT variants, HALT-L and HALT-Q, trained respectively on Llama 3.1-8B and Qwen 2.5-7B log-probabilities. While being 30x smaller, HALT outperforms fine-tuned baselines and provides a 60x speed gain on HUB HALT and HUB throughout.

key_findings.finding: Macro-averaged F1 on HUB shows HALT-L achieves 63.04 across nine capability clusters, with particularly strong performance on knowledge-heavy tasks (Data2Text 83.38, QA 77.30) but lower performance on reasoning (Code Generation 47.67).
key_findings.quote: Table 2 reports macro-F1 across HUB clusters. We compare aggregated statistics, the span-based Lettuce detector, and our two HALT variants. Lettuce performs strongly on knowledge-heavy clusters such as Data2Text (83.38) and QA (77.30), but lags on reasoning tasks where sequence-level calibration cues are more predictive.

key_findings.finding: HALT demonstrates model-specific calibration bias that does not transfer reliably across LLMs; cross-model transfer (HALT-L trained on LLaMA to Qwen, HALT-Q to LLaMA) produces substantial AUROC drops from 70.02 to 55.24 and 61.11, supporting the finding that calibration dynamics are not reliably transferable across models.
key_findings.quote: Importantly, both HALT variants outperform Lettuce and all randomized or trivial baselines. Cross-model transfer (HALT-L -> Qwen, HALT-Q -> LLaMA LogProbs) produces substantial drops, directly supporting Hypothesis 3 that calibration dynamics are not reliably transferable across models.

relation_to_herald.shared: Both use per-token log-probability signals for failure prediction without requiring access to model internals Both treat token-level signals as informative patterns rather than aggregate confidence statistics Both position themselves as black-box or brown-box approaches compatible with proprietary LLM APIs
differs_on: HALT targets general hallucinations (factual errors, logical inconsistencies, reasoning failures) during normal inference; HERALD targets compression-induced catastrophic failures (looping, non-termination, instruction drift) specific to KV-cache eviction
HALT uses a GRU recurrent architecture for temporal sequence modeling; HERALD uses XGBoost with engineered features

HALT demonstrates poor cross-model transferability (substantial AUROC drops across different LLMs); HERALD's transferability across compression methods and models is not similarly constrained by calibration bias differences
